title: Video: Trump In Asia
gist: Gavekal's Tom Miller argues the Xi-Trump-Putin trilateral and Trump-Xi bilateral at APEC Shenzhen were high political theatre with no market-moving substance (no trade-truce extension past Jan 10, no rare-earth or Ukraine/Iran breakthroughs), but the meetings mattered as signals: legitimacy for Putin, a lame-duck Trump acting abroad, and a more conciliatory yet chip-control-driven US recommitment to Asia via ASEAN, the Philippines and the Quad.

themes.theme: Xi-Trump-Putin trilateral: theatre, not a new Yalta

insights.claim: Gavekal's Tom Miller judges the first Xi-Trump-Putin trilateral (90 minutes on the APEC Shenzhen sidelines) produced no concrete outcomes on Ukraine, the Iran war or nuclear disarmament, making 'new Yalta' comparisons overdone.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Do not trade the trilateral as a geopolitical regime shift; headline risk outran substance.
insights.quote: there were no concrete outcomes on Ukraine, on the Iran war, on nuclear disarmament
insights.locator: But there were no concrete outcomes on Ukraine

insights.claim: At the trilateral Xi Jinping showed little interest in being drawn into Ukraine, and Iran was discussed but omitted from the final declaration because China does not want involvement in a Middle Eastern war.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: China will not act as a broker on Ukraine or Iran; do not price Chinese-led peace dividends.
insights.locator: So if you look at the major issues on Ukraine

insights.claim: Xi Jinping called for prohibiting nuclear weapons while the Pentagon projects China's nuclear warhead stockpile will exceed 1,000 by 2030, as China builds faster than anyone to catch up with the US and Russia.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Chinese disarmament rhetoric contradicts its build-out; arms-race dynamics support long-run defence spending.
insights.quote: The Pentagon projects that China's stockpile of nuclear warheads will exceed 1,000 by 2030.
insights.locator: And then on the nuclear issue

insights.claim: Rather than birthing a new international order, the trilateral undermined the old one: the three leaders pledged UN reform and attacked the International Criminal Court.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Erosion of multilateral institutions raises background geopolitical risk premia without a replacement framework.
insights.quote: What we're seeing really is more the undermining of the old one.
insights.locator: What we're seeing really is more the undermining

insights.claim: The trilateral cemented China's image as a prime global player, with Xi positioned in the middle as Roosevelt was at Yalta, even though China does not want the responsibility of running the world.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: China's status gains are symbolic; don't expect Beijing to underwrite global security burdens.
insights.locator: What it did do, I suppose, is cement the image

insights.claim: The trilateral's announced increase in refined petroleum product supply barely moved oil: Brent ticked up very slightly, because Trump had already suspended most Russia-related tariffs and Lindsey Graham Act sanctions and the US Treasury had granted a six-month waiver on Russian diesel trade.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Russian sanction relief was already priced; the summit added no incremental supply shock to oil or diesel.
insights.locator: And, you know, it really wasn't a market moving event

insights.claim: The Trump-Xi bilateral delivered no extension of the US-China trade truce beyond January 10 and no breakthroughs on rare earths, tech exports, tariffs or Chinese purchases, deferring decisions to a Miami meeting next month.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: January 10 truce expiry and the Miami meeting are the next real US-China trade catalysts to watch.
insights.quote: There was no extension of the trade truce beyond January the 10th.
insights.locator: If you look at the Trump's Xi Jinping bilateral

insights.claim: The US-China Board of Trade was formally established and held its first meeting, creating a dedicated mechanism for managing trade disputes.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: An institutional dispute channel modestly lowers tail risk of abrupt tariff escalation.
insights.locator: We did see the formal establishment of the Board of Trade

insights.claim: Gavekal reads the Trump-Xi meeting as mainly a massaging of Trump's ego, which may help keep US-China relations on track for the rest of his presidency.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Supports a base case of relative US-China stability through Trump's term.
insights.quote: what we really saw was a massaging of Trump's ego
insights.locator: So what we really saw was a massaging

insights.claim: The meeting conferred legitimacy and global status on Putin; as Trump's second meeting with him since the Ukraine invasion, it suggests Trump may put further pressure on Ukraine and make more concessions to Russia.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Raises odds of further Russia sanction relief and Ukraine-unfavourable settlement terms — relevant for European energy and defence.
insights.locator: So it did confer legitimacy and global status on Putin

insights.claim: Weakened by midterm losses and the Jensen Huang spy controversy, Trump may be a lame duck at home but can still act abroad, where Congress has little power, and is motivated to pursue grand legacy gestures such as peace in Ukraine or Iran.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Expect foreign-policy volatility (deals, gestures) to rise even as domestic policy stalls.
insights.quote: a lame duck president can still act abroad
insights.locator: It was also important, I think, because of the context at home

insights.claim: Xi Jinping sometimes skips the G20 and the UN General Assembly but never skips APEC, signalling how seriously China treats the forum.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: APEC is Beijing's preferred platform for economic diplomacy; watch its outputs for Chinese trade-policy signalling.
insights.locator: I mean, it's worth noting, I think, that Xi Jinping

themes.theme: APEC Shenzhen: free-trade rhetoric vs reality

insights.claim: China used APEC to project itself as a responsible free-trade champion and more reliable partner than the US, yet it is itself withholding some exports of rare earth permanent magnets.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Rare-earth magnet supply remains a live Chinese lever; supports non-China rare-earth/magnet supply chains.
insights.quote: it's hardly the paragon of free trade that it likes to project
insights.locator: But what it was, though, was an opportunity for Xi

insights.claim: APEC's Shenzhen Outlook communique called for supply-chain resilience and addressing economic choke points, and reaffirmed a Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific that Gavekal calls a politically impossible pipe dream.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Ignore FTAAP headlines; regional trade integration will not offset US protectionism.
insights.locator: What we did have was the so-called Shenzhen Outlook

insights.claim: On APEC's sidelines Xi Jinping and Canada's Carney extended tariff relief, putting China-Canada relations back on track as Canada diversifies trade away from the US; a similar thaw is underway with Australia's Albanese.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: US allies hedging toward China benefits Canadian/Australian exporters to China (e.g., agriculture, resources).
insights.locator: When it comes to substantive things

themes.theme: US recommitment to Asia, with chip-control strings

insights.claim: Trump attending ASEAN for a second straight year (versus one meeting in his first term and Biden skipping 2023 and 2024) signals sustained US attention to Asia, and this trip was more conciliatory and less nakedly transactional than last year's tariff-heavy visit.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Reduced US coercion lowers tariff-shock risk for Southeast Asian exporters near term.
insights.locator: So, this is the second year that Trump has attended

insights.claim: Thailand is close to a US trade deal that would eliminate tariffs on 99% of US goods, showing Trump's Asia approach remains transactional beneath the friendlier tone.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Watch the Thailand deal as a template for ASEAN tariff concessions to the US.
insights.locator: Thailand, for example, is close to closing a trade deal

insights.claim: The US-ASEAN Special Summit produced a five-year cooperation package covering maritime security, digital infrastructure, emerging technologies, critical minerals and energy, framed as part of getting tough on China.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Supports US-aligned critical-minerals and digital-infrastructure investment in Southeast Asia.
insights.locator: So the first one was the U.S. ASEAN Special Summit

insights.claim: The new US crackdown on chip exports and compute rental in third countries targets Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia, pushing aspiring neutral data-centre hubs to police Chinese customers; Singapore's Lawrence Wong said Singapore will facilitate chip trade checks but not enforce US export controls.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Southeast Asian data-centre growth faces compliance friction; Chinese access to compute via third countries is being squeezed but not closed.
insights.quote: Singapore will facilitate trade checks on chips, but it will not enforce U.S. export controls
insights.locator: And I think here it's worth pointing out that Trump

insights.claim: The Philippines under Marcos has moved back into alignment with the US; Trump reaffirmed defence commitments, and Washington has approved $5 billion of fighter jet and arms sales over two years that Manila cannot actually afford.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Arms approvals overstate realizable US defence exports to Manila; financing is the constraint.
insights.locator: I think the other, the second important meeting

insights.claim: The Quad (US, India, Japan, Australia), thought killed off by Trump's tariffs on India after the Delhi leaders meeting was cancelled, met again and launched a maritime surveillance initiative, joint military exercises and thin cooperation on critical minerals and AI supply chains.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Quad revival signals the US remains committed to Asian security, supportive of regional defence cooperation.
insights.locator: And then I think the final thing to look at is the Quad
